symptom: congestion-driven routing DRCs with clean placement density

first_checks.check: Compare global-route congestion by layer and region against pin-access / local-routing demand, not just cell utilization.
first_checks.why_first: cheapest way to distinguish true area overflow from a localized routing-resource or pin-access bottleneck

first_checks.check: Overlay DRC locations with macro edges, blockages, power straps, clock routes, and high-fanout/bus corridors.
first_checks.why_first: quickly identifies whether nominally empty area is actually unavailable routing capacity

first_checks.check: Run a short trial route after temporarily relaxing or removing the suspected blockage/NDR constraint.
first_checks.why_first: directly tests whether the constraint, rather than placement density, is consuming the missing resources

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Temporarily remove the dominant routing blockage/NDR and rerun trial routing; compare overflow/DRC concentration.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: If the hotspot largely disappears or migrates, routing constraints/resource reservation are confirmed as the dominant cause.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If the hotspot remains essentially unchanged, the blockage is unlikely to be the primary cause.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run a pin-access-focused route or inspect access failures with standard-cell placement frozen; compare failures before and after small local cell spreading.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: If a few rows/macros become routable after tiny local spreading despite unchanged global density, local pin access is confirmed.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If spreading has little effect but changing layer capacity does, pin access is unlikely to be primary.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare congestion with clock/power routing included versus a signal-only trial route.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: A large reduction when special nets are excluded implicates reserved/consumed routing resources.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Little change implicates ordinary signal demand or pin-access geometry instead.

common_root_causes.cause: Local routing-resource bottleneck from macros, blockages, power grid, or layer restrictions
Pin-access / cell-boundary geometry creating severe local demand despite acceptable placement density
High-fanout buses or concentrated connectivity creating directional routing demand
Clock or non-default routing consuming resources unexpectedly
Fundamental placement-density problem despite apparently clean aggregate utilization

classic_trap: Treating clean average utilization as proof of routability and immediately spreading the whole block, when the actual problem is often a small routing-resource or pin-access hotspot.
node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, restrictive pitches, via rules, pin access, and advanced routing rules make local routability less correlated with aggregate density than it was at 28nm.

first_checks.check: Classify failing paths by launch/capture clock pair, physical region, and whether the dominant delay is cell or interconnect.
first_checks.why_first: fastest split between a clock-domain/clock-skew problem and a data-path problem

first_checks.check: Compare the same paths pre-CTS versus post-CTS using propagated clocks.
first_checks.why_first: isolates whether CTS itself introduced the regression

first_checks.check: Check whether many failures share common clock-tree branches, clock-gating cells, or a single physical corridor.
first_checks.why_first: common clock ancestry can turn thousands of apparent data failures into one CTS issue

first_checks.check: Check extracted/estimated RC and transition on the worst data nets.
first_checks.why_first: distinguishes physical interconnect degradation from insufficient logical drive

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Recompute the same failing paths with ideal clocks versus propagated CTS clocks.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: If setup recovers substantially with ideal clocks, clock latency/skew is a live primary cause; if not, the data path remains primary.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If the violation is nearly unchanged, CTS skew is unlikely to explain the regression.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Temporarily resize only the worst data-path cells versus perturbing the capture clock branch; compare slack recovery per change.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Large recovery from data-path changes implicates data delay; disproportionate recovery from capture-clock movement implicates skew/latency.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: No meaningful response to either suggests constraints, mode/corner, or a broader RC problem.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare pre-CTS and post-CTS path topology for a sample spanning unrelated hierarchies.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Failures appearing across unrelated data paths but sharing a clock branch point toward a common CTS problem.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Failures confined to physically long/high-fanout paths with unchanged clock behavior point toward data-path RC.

common_root_causes.cause: Clock skew/latency distribution changed effective setup budget
Long or congested post-CTS data interconnect increased RC delay
Insufficient drive / poor transition on critical data paths
CTS buffering and clock routing consumed nearby routing resources, indirectly degrading data paths
Constraint, mode, corner, or propagated-clock interpretation issue

classic_trap: Upsizing every failing data path before checking whether the failures share a clock-tree cause; this can burn power and congestion while leaving the real problem intact.
node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, post-CTS setup is more tightly coupled to extracted interconnect, SI, and congestion than in older-node designs.

first_checks.check: Compare pre-CTS ideal-clock hold against post-CTS propagated-clock hold for the same endpoints.
first_checks.why_first: immediately establishes whether real clock skew created the new failures

first_checks.check: Cluster failures by clock skew and common launch/capture clock-tree branches.
first_checks.why_first: hold failures frequently have a common clock-side signature

first_checks.check: Check whether failing data paths are extremely short and whether delay cells/buffers were removed or optimized away.
first_checks.why_first: short paths are the simplest competing explanation

first_checks.check: Check whether hold fixing is itself creating routing/congestion pressure.
first_checks.why_first: prevents a local timing repair from becoming a physical-design failure elsewhere

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Replace propagated clocks with ideal clocks while holding the data implementation fixed.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: If most violations disappear, CTS skew/latency is confirmed as the dominant trigger.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If they persist, short data-path delay rather than CTS is likely dominant.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Perturb only the capture-clock branch latency in a controlled CTS experiment.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: If small capture-clock delay changes produce the expected large hold-slack movement across the cluster, clock skew is confirmed.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If hold slack barely responds, the data path is the stronger hypothesis.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Insert delay on a representative failing data path without changing clocks and compare hold recovery.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Strong recovery with localized data delay confirms insufficient minimum data delay.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Little recovery points toward clock-side or constraint causes.

common_root_causes.cause: Positive clock skew / unequal CTS insertion delay creating short effective hold windows
Very short data paths requiring deliberate delay
Clock-gating or generated-clock topology producing unexpected local skew
Constraint or clock-definition issue
Hold-fix optimization creating secondary congestion or timing interactions

classic_trap: Adding delay buffers everywhere without first checking whether the same clock-tree branch explains a large fraction of the violations.
node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, very small cell/interconnect delays and tighter skew margins make extracted RC and variation more important to hold closure.

first_checks.check: Correlate the failing timing endpoints with static and dynamic IR-drop maps at the same physical locations and operating condition.
first_checks.why_first: cheapest direct test of whether voltage loss spatially overlaps the timing failure

first_checks.check: Compare timing with nominal versus voltage-aware cell libraries or voltage-drop-aware analysis.
first_checks.why_first: separates genuine voltage sensitivity from ordinary RC timing failure

first_checks.check: Inspect local power-grid topology, rail access, strap density, vias, and nearby switching-current concentration.
first_checks.why_first: identifies the physical mechanism behind a localized droop

first_checks.check: Compare failing paths against activity scenarios rather than only average chip current.
first_checks.why_first: dynamic droop is often localized and workload-dependent

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Re-run timing under nominal voltage and under the extracted voltage-drop map while keeping placement/routes unchanged.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: A substantial slack loss only under voltage-aware analysis confirms IR-induced timing degradation.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If timing remains nearly identical, IR drop is unlikely to be the cause.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Temporarily strengthen the local power grid with additional nearby supply access/vias in a copy and rerun IR/timing.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: If local voltage and timing recover together, insufficient local power delivery is confirmed.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If voltage improves but timing does not, the timing failure likely has another dominant cause.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare static versus dynamic IR results for the failing region under several activity scenarios.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Failure appearing only under high simultaneous switching implicates dynamic IR.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Failure persisting similarly under low activity points toward static resistance or a non-IR timing issue.

common_root_causes.cause: Localized power-grid resistance / insufficient straps or vias
High local switching current density
Voltage-drop sensitivity of already marginal critical cells
Power-grid interaction with macro channels or sparse rail access
Analysis/activity mismatch rather than actual silicon-relevant droop

classic_trap: Blaming the data path for a timing regression without checking whether its cells sit in the IR hotspot; IR and timing are coupled through the local supply voltage.
node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, lower voltages and higher current density make IR-drop/timing coupling substantially more prominent than at 28nm.

symptom: clock skew / CTS divergence (sinks missing insertion-delay targets)

first_checks.check: Cluster bad sinks by clock-tree branch and physical region, then compare actual versus target insertion delay.
first_checks.why_first: common ancestry quickly distinguishes a local branch problem from a global CTS problem

first_checks.check: Check clock-net congestion and whether the intended routing layers/resources are available around the divergent branches.
first_checks.why_first: routing scarcity is a common physical reason a nominal CTS topology cannot realize its target

first_checks.check: Check clock-gating cells, macro boundaries, blockages, and sink exclusions around the affected subtree.
first_checks.why_first: these often explain why only a subset of sinks diverges

first_checks.check: Inspect transition/fanout and buffer sizing on the first divergent branch.
first_checks.why_first: identifies electrical loading before changing the entire tree

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare a failing subtree with an otherwise similar good subtree sharing the same source, using physical distance and branch depth as controls.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: If only the physically constrained subtree diverges, local routing/blockage/loading is implicated.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If divergence begins at the common upstream branch, the problem is upstream of the subtree.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run CTS with the local routing blockage/resource constraint temporarily relaxed.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: If insertion delay and skew recover, routing-resource availability is confirmed as the constraint.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If the same subtree still misses target, look at electrical loading, constraints, or topology.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Temporarily reduce sink fanout or isolate a representative divergent branch and compare insertion delay.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Large improvement implicates excessive loading/buffering topology.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Little change points toward physical routing or clock constraints.

common_root_causes.cause: Local clock-routing congestion or blockage
Unexpected clock-tree topology caused by gating, macros, or sink grouping
High fanout / transition and insufficient buffering
Clock constraints or sink-definition errors
Variation/SI effects causing signoff divergence from CTS estimates

classic_trap: Treating all bad sinks as one global CTS problem and rebuilding the whole tree instead of finding the first common branch where the divergence begins.
node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, clock routing, variation, SI, and restrictive upper-metal resources make CTS/signoff divergence more tightly coupled to detailed physical implementation.

symptom: LVS mismatch: missing / shorted / open nets

first_checks.check: Determine whether the mismatch is logical connectivity, extracted geometry, or source/netlist correspondence before inspecting layout manually.
first_checks.why_first: narrows the search space before expensive polygon-level debugging

first_checks.check: Locate the first unmatched net and inspect its immediate vias, contacts, pin shapes, and neighboring conductors.
first_checks.why_first: opens and shorts are usually localized to a small physical region

first_checks.check: Compare the layout-versus-source connectivity around the first mismatch rather than chasing every downstream mismatch.
first_checks.why_first: one upstream open/short often creates many secondary mismatches

first_checks.check: Check whether the failing geometry came from a recent ECO or incremental route.
first_checks.why_first: recent physical edits are disproportionately useful suspects

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run LVS after removing the suspect ECO geometry while leaving the logical netlist unchanged.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: If the original connectivity mismatch disappears, the ECO geometry is confirmed as the source.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If it persists, the mismatch is upstream or unrelated to that edit.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare extracted connectivity with a connectivity-only layout check before full LVS.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: If connectivity is already wrong, the issue is physical geometry/via/contact connectivity.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If connectivity is correct but LVS still differs, investigate device/source correspondence or extraction interpretation.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Inspect whether multiple reported net mismatches collapse to one location when the first unmatched net is corrected.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: Collapse of many errors after one correction confirms a primary open/short rather than independent failures.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Independent mismatches remaining indicate multiple physical defects or a source/extraction issue.

common_root_causes.cause: Missing/bad via or contact causing an open
Metal spacing/geometry or accidental overlap causing a short
Pin-shape/connectivity mismatch at a cell or macro boundary
ECO routing/geometry error
Extraction/source-netlist interpretation mismatch

classic_trap: Fixing every LVS mismatch independently when one missing via or short can generate a large cascade of secondary net mismatches.
node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, dense via structures and more restrictive multi-pattern/multi-cut rules make small via/connectivity mistakes especially consequential.

symptom: LVS mismatch: wrong device sizes or extra devices

first_checks.check: Determine whether the mismatch is isolated to one cell/device or repeated systematically across a library/master.
first_checks.why_first: a repeated signature strongly suggests a source/library extraction issue rather than random layout damage

first_checks.check: Compare extracted device parameters against the intended master/layout generator parameters for one representative mismatch.
first_checks.why_first: quickly distinguishes geometry-sizing error from incorrect source expectation

first_checks.check: Check recent library, PDK, or layout-generator changes and whether source and layout used matching versions.
first_checks.why_first: version skew can create systematic mismatches

first_checks.check: Inspect transistor geometry only after establishing whether the mismatch is systematic or isolated.
first_checks.why_first: avoids wasting time manually debugging hundreds of identical devices

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare several mismatched devices with the same nominal master but different physical instances.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: If extracted sizes are consistently shifted in the same way, a master/PDK/extraction interpretation issue is likely.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If only one instance differs, a local layout geometry error is more likely.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run extraction/LVS against a known-good revision of the same standard-cell or macro master.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: If the mismatch disappears with the known-good master, the changed library/layout is implicated.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If it persists, investigate source netlist or extraction rules.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Replace one suspect physical instance with the unmodified reference master and rerun LVS.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: If the mismatch disappears, local cell geometry is confirmed.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If the mismatch remains, the problem is likely outside that device geometry.

common_root_causes.cause: Incorrect or changed standard-cell/macro layout geometry
Source netlist versus physical library/master version mismatch
PDK/extraction rule interpretation of device dimensions
ECO accidentally adding/removing or resizing physical devices
True isolated transistor geometry error

classic_trap: Assuming every wrong-device-size report means someone physically drew the transistor wrong, when systematic mismatches often originate in master, PDK, or source-version mismatch.
node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, device recognition and multi-pattern/fin-based geometry make PDK/extraction interpretation more coupled to the physical representation than in planar 28nm practice.

first_checks.check: Cluster antenna violations by layer, net, and standard-cell pin/gate type.
first_checks.why_first: quickly distinguishes a systematic layer/rule problem from isolated long-net geometry

first_checks.check: Inspect whether the offending net has a very long metal segment before a higher-layer jump or diffusion connection.
first_checks.why_first: the physical shape often makes the antenna mechanism immediately obvious

first_checks.check: Check whether the process deck permits a jumper or diode solution and which part of the net contributes to the reported ratio.
first_checks.why_first: identifies the cheapest physically legal repair

first_checks.check: Check whether the violations were introduced by a recent ECO or final routing optimization.
first_checks.why_first: recent route changes are a strong localization clue

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Insert a legal higher-layer metal jump on a representative offending net and rerun antenna verification.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: If the antenna ratio drops below the rule threshold, accumulated lower-layer geometry is confirmed as the cause.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If the violation remains, the offending contribution is elsewhere in the net or the chosen repair is ineffective.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Add a representative antenna diode to one failing net and rerun the check.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: If the violation clears without changing routing geometry, gate-area/charge-collection is confirmed and diode repair is viable.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If it does not clear, inspect the reported antenna contribution and rule interpretation.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Compare signoff antenna results before and after the last routing/ECO delta.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: New violations confined to modified nets implicate the routing change.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Violations present identically before the delta indicate an earlier routing or rule issue.

common_root_causes.cause: Long lower-metal segment connected to a sensitive gate before a protective layer transition
Routing topology creating excessive antenna ratio on particular nets
Late ECO or detailed-routing change introducing an antenna-prone geometry
Missing/ineffective antenna diode or jumper opportunity
Rule-deck or layer-recognition interpretation issue

classic_trap: Treating antenna as an ordinary DRC spacing problem and moving wires locally, rather than addressing the process-specific accumulated conductor-to-gate ratio.
node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, more complex routing stacks and process-specific antenna rules make layer choice and jumper strategy more significant than at 28nm.

symptom: detailed-routing DRC hotspots after clean global routing

first_checks.check: Map detailed DRCs by exact rule type and layer before looking at aggregate violation count.
first_checks.why_first: a single rule/layer signature often identifies the physical bottleneck immediately

first_checks.check: Check whether violations cluster at pin access, via transitions, macro boundaries, or track intersections.
first_checks.why_first: these are the usual places where global-route feasibility fails at exact geometry

first_checks.check: Compare the detailed-route result against the global-route guide around the hotspot.
first_checks.why_first: tests whether detailed routing is failing to realize an otherwise feasible global solution

first_checks.check: Inspect nearby NDRs, shielding, double-patterning/coloring, and special-net reservations.
first_checks.why_first: special constraints can invalidate globally legal-looking routes

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Reroute one hotspot with relaxed local route constraints while keeping the global route guide fixed.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: If detailed DRCs clear, the local routing constraint or preferred geometry is the cause.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If DRCs persist at the same shapes, the issue is likely fundamental pin/via geometry or technology rules.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Temporarily route the hotspot on adjacent layers with fewer restrictive rules.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: If the hotspot clears when layer choice changes, layer-specific capacity/rules are confirmed.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If the same violation follows the geometry across layers, investigate pin/via or rule interactions.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Disable a suspected NDR/shielding requirement for a single experimental net and compare DRCs.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: A large local reduction confirms the special routing requirement is consuming incompatible geometry.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: No change makes that NDR less likely to be the primary cause.

common_root_causes.cause: Pin-access conflicts and dense local via geometry
Layer-specific spacing/via/width rules not captured accurately by global routing
NDR, shielding, or special-net interaction
Macro/blockage boundary geometry
Manufacturing-specific rules such as coloring or restrictive patterning interactions

classic_trap: Assuming clean global routing means the region is physically routable, when detailed routing still has to satisfy exact-track, via, pin-access, and manufacturing geometry constraints.
node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, detailed-route failures are more strongly dominated by pin access, via rules, coloring, and restrictive geometry than at 28nm.

symptom: unroutable placement (global placement diverges or overflows)

first_checks.check: Check global placement overflow/convergence together with local density and routing congestion maps.
first_checks.why_first: separates a numerical placement failure from a physical-resource failure

first_checks.check: Inspect macro placement, halos, channels, blockages, and major high-fanout connectivity.
first_checks.why_first: macro topology can create impossible routing demand even when average utilization looks reasonable

first_checks.check: Temporarily reduce target utilization or spread cells and rerun a short placement experiment.
first_checks.why_first: cheap controlled test of whether the problem is simply insufficient whitespace

first_checks.check: Compare placement behavior with major timing/physical constraints relaxed.
first_checks.why_first: reveals whether competing objectives are causing optimizer instability

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run placement at substantially lower utilization while keeping floorplan and constraints otherwise unchanged.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: If placement converges and routing overflow falls sharply, insufficient whitespace/resource capacity is confirmed.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If divergence persists, utilization alone is not the primary cause.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Temporarily remove or relax macro halos/blockages in a copy and rerun placement.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: A large improvement implicates floorplan restrictions rather than intrinsic cell count.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Little change points toward connectivity, constraints, or optimizer pathology.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Run placement with major timing-driven objectives relaxed and compare convergence/overflow.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: If placement stabilizes when timing pressure is removed, conflicting timing/routability objectives are implicated.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: If overflow remains similar, the root is likely physical capacity or floorplan.

discriminating_experiments.experiment: Partition congestion by region and correlate overflow with high-fanout nets and macro interfaces.
discriminating_experiments.rules_in: A few dominant regions/nets causing most overflow implicate topology/connectivity rather than uniformly excessive density.
discriminating_experiments.rules_out: Uniform overflow across the core points more strongly to global capacity/utilization.

common_root_causes.cause: Excessive effective utilization / insufficient whitespace
Poor macro placement, channels, halos, or blockages
High-fanout / long-range connectivity creating impossible routing demand
Conflicting timing, congestion, and physical constraints
Bad floorplan or aspect-ratio assumptions forcing pathological placement

classic_trap: Responding to placement overflow by globally increasing whitespace without first identifying whether a handful of macros, blockages, or connectivity corridors are creating the real bottleneck.
node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, lower routing pitch, restrictive pin access, and advanced-node routing rules make placement routability more sensitive to local geometry than at 28nm.
